citeAs: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (2021). Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset. NeurIPS 2021 Track on Datasets and Benchmarks.
creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt (UC Berkeley)
description: MATH is a dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems (7,500 training and 5,000 test) drawn from competitions including the AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME. Each problem includes a full step-by-step solution written in LaTeX and natural language, and a final boxed answer. Problems are tagged by difficulty level (1–5) and span seven subjects: Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus.
name: MATH
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Problems are tagged by difficulty from 1 to 5, following AoPS conventions. A subject's easiest problems are assigned difficulty level 1 and hardest problems level 5. Problems span seven subjects: Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus. Each problem includes a full step-by-step solution and a final boxed answer.
rai:dataCollection: Problems were collected from mathematics competitions including the AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and more, many sourced from aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests. These competitions span decades and assess the mathematical problem-solving ability of the best young mathematical talent in the United States.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Competition mathematics problems from AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and other competitions, collected from aops.com. Problems include step-by-step solutions and final answers, formatted in LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is not intended to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams. Even 40% accuracy for a machine learning model would have ramifications for cheating on homework.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems and solutions are consistently formatted using LaTeX and the Asymptote vector graphics language. Final boxed answers follow consistent formatting rules: probabilities expressed as simplified fractions; matrix entry fractions encoded with x/y; other fractions with \frac{x}{y}; coefficients without multiplication symbol; expressions with multiple variables in alphabetical order; polynomials in decreasing degree order. Equivalent representations (e.g., 0.5 and 1/2) are treated as the same.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to advance mathematical reasoning in ML models. The authors note that achieving strong performance on MATH would be of profound practical and intellectual significance given the broad reach of mathematics. However, high model accuracy could have ramifications for cheating on homework and mathematics exams.
rai:dataUseCases: Benchmarking mathematical problem-solving ability of machine learning models; training models to generate step-by-step answer derivations and explanations; measuring and forecasting reasoning capabilities of large language models.

evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: To assess models using exact match, we force the final boxed answers to follow consistent formatting rules. Specifically, probabilities are expressed as simplified fractions. Moreover, matrix entry fractions are encoded with x/y, while all other fractions are consistently encoded with the \frac{x}{y} command. Coefficients are encoded without a multiplication symbol (e.g. 5x not 5*x). Expressions with multiple variables are entered in alphabetical order; polynomials are expressed in decreasing degree order.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: We encode a problem's difficulty level from '1' to '5,' following AoPS. A subject's easiest problems for humans are assigned a difficulty level of '1,' and a subject's hardest problems are assigned a difficulty level of '5.' Concretely, the first few problems of an AMC 8 exam are often level 1, while AIME problems are level 5.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: Dataset Intended Uses. We document the dataset within the paper and note that the dataset and code for reproducing results is available at https://github.com/hendrycks/apps. We do not intend for this dataset to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams. We intend for others to use this dataset in order to better forecast reasoning capabilities.
evidence.rai:dataLimitations: We do not intend for this dataset to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams. We intend for others to use this dataset in order to better forecast reasoning capabilities. Expert-level performance is theoretically 100% given enough time. Even 40% would accuracy for a machine learning model would be impressive but have ramifications for cheating on homework.
evidence.rai:dataSocialImpact: Given the broad reach and applicability of mathematics, solving the MATH dataset with machine learning would be of profound practical and intellectual significance. We do not intend for this dataset to train models that help students cheat on mathematics exams.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: Because MATH requires a strong mathematical background to perform well on, and a long amount of time to solve problems, we were restricted to assessing six human participants and could not rely on crowdsourcing sites such as Amazon Mechanical Turk. All participants are university students studying computer science. Four of the participants are authors on the paper. The other two participants are friends or acquaintances of the authors.
